metadata.title: Developments in Formal Proofs

extraction_notes.note: Formal statements given only as code listings (Coq/HOL/Isabelle: Feit_Thompson, isconnBG, Four-Color, PNT, Brouwer, CLT, Kepler, isogeny) are not nodes: they are not prose sentences; the prose context sentences were used where they state the result.
The three-paragraph outline of the Feit-Thompson proof was emitted as a proof of TP2 (a sketch, not a full argument) rather than a remark, since it justifies the separately stated theorem.

Theorem 1 is a 'routine exercise' made external (standard, uncited), which forbids rigor; its proof is labelled a sketch but the proof-sketch rigor rule applies only to results proved elsewhere, so no rigor field was set.
The ten HOL inference rules in the appendix were typed as definitions (they constitute the deductive system) rather than assumptions.

metadata.extraction_comment: A Bourbaki-seminar survey: most content is discursive; nodes cover the HOL model construction, the two theorem environments, and the definitions and procedures stated in prose.

nodes.name: simple type system
nodes.statement: Naively, a simple type system is a countable collection of disjoint nonempty sets called types.
nodes.genus: countable collection of disjoint nonempty sets

nodes.name: function type $A\to B$
nodes.statement: The collection of types satisfies a closure property: for every two types $A$ and $B$, there is a further type, denoted $A\to B$, that can be identified with the set of functions from $A$ to $B$.

nodes.name: terms
nodes.statement: In addition to types, there are terms, which are thought of as elements of types.

nodes.name: typing relation $t:A$
nodes.statement: Each term $t$ has a unique type $A$. This relationship between a term and its type is denoted $t:A$. In particular, $f:A\to B$ denotes a term $f$ of type $A\to B$.

nodes.name: type variables
nodes.statement: There are variables that range over types called {\it type variables}, and another collection of variables that run over terms.

nodes.name: interpretation superscript $M$
nodes.statement: We use a superscript $M$ to mark the interpretation of a type as a set.

nodes.name: interpretation of base types bool and I
nodes.statement: Specifically, the types in HOL are generated by the boolean type $\op{\tt bool}$ (which we interpret as a set $\op{\tt bool}^M=\{\downvdash ,\upvdash \}$ of cardinality two with labeled elements representing true and false) and the infinite type $I$ (which we interpret as a countably infinite set $I^M$).
nodes.statement_short: HOL types are generated by bool (a two-element set) and an infinite type I (a countably infinite set).

nodes.name: interpretation of function types
nodes.statement: Recursively, for any two variable-free types $A$ and $B$, the type $A\to B$ is interpreted as the set $(A\to B)^M$ of all functions from $A^M$ to $B^M$.

nodes.name: collection of type interpretations $\mathcal T$
nodes.statement: In summary so far, we fix an interpretation $M$, determining a countable collection ${\mathcal T} =\{A^M\}$ of nonempty sets in ZFC.

nodes.name: valuation
nodes.statement: We now extend our interpretation $M$ to a {\it valuation} $v=(M,v_1,v_2)$, where $v_1$ is a function from the set of type variables in HOL to ${\mathcal T}$, and $v_2$ is a function from the set of term variables in HOL to $\bigcup{\mathcal T}$.
nodes.statement_short: A valuation extends M with assignments of type variables to sets in T and term variables to elements of their union.

nodes.name: valuation of types $A^v$
nodes.statement: The valuation $v$ extends recursively to give a mapping that assigns a set $A^{v}\in {\mathcal T}$ to every type $A$. We require $v_2$ to be chosen so that whenever $x$ is a variable of type $A$, then $x^{v_2} \in A^v$.

nodes.name: valuation of terms $t^v$
nodes.statement: The valuation $v$ extends recursively to give a mapping on all terms: \[ t\mapsto t^v \in A^v \in {\mathcal T}, \quad \text{for all } t:A. \]

nodes.name: HOL equality term $(=)$
nodes.statement: For example, for every type $A$, there is a HOL term $(=)$ of type $A\to (A\to \op{\tt bool})$ representing equality for that type.\footnote{The convention in HOL is to curry functions: using the bijection $X^{Y \times Z} = (X^Z)^Y$ to write a function whose domain is a product as a function of a single argument taking values in a function space. In particular, equality is a curried function of type $A\to (A \to\op{\tt bool})$ rather than a relation on $A\times A$.}

nodes.name: interpretation of equality
nodes.statement: This term is interpreted as the function in $(A\to (A\to\op{\tt bool}))^v$ that maps $a\in A^{v}$ to the delta function $\delta_a$ supported at $a$ (where the support of the function means the preimage of $\downvdash$).
nodes.statement_short: Equality at type A is interpreted as the map sending a to the delta function supported at a.

nodes.name: sequent
nodes.statement: A {\it sequent} is a pair $(L,t)$, traditionally written $L\vdash t$, where $L$ is a finite set of terms called the {\it assumptions}, and $t$ is a term called the {\it conclusion}. The terms of $L$ and $t$ must all have type $\op{\tt bool}$. If $L$ is empty, it is omitted from the notation.
differentia: $L$ is a finite set of terms called the {\it assumptions}
$t$ is a term called the {\it conclusion}

nodes.name: $L^v$
nodes.statement: If $L$ is a finite set of boolean terms, and if $v$ is a valuation extending $M$, write $L^{v}$ for the corresponding set of elements of the set $\op{\tt bool}^M$.

nodes.name: logically valid sequent
nodes.statement: We say a sequent $L \vdash t$ is {\it logically valid} if for every valuation $v$ for which every element of $L^{v}$ is $\downvdash \in \op{\tt bool}^M$, we also have $t^{v}=\downvdash $ in $\op{\tt bool}^M$.

nodes.name: theorem in HOL
nodes.statement: A {\it theorem} in HOL is a sequent that is generated from the mathematical axioms and rules of logic.
differentia: generated from the mathematical axioms and rules of logic

nodes.name: Consistency of HOL relative to ZFC
nodes.statement: If ZFC is consistent, then HOL is consistent.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the consistency of HOL
nodes.statement: We give the proof in ZFC. Here, HOL is treated purely syntactically as a set of strings in a formal language. We run through the rules of logic of HOL one by one and check that each one preserves validity.\footnote{There are ten such rules, giving the behavior of equality, $\lambda$-abstractions, $\beta$-reduction, and the discharge of assumptions. For reference purposes, an appendix lists the inference rules of HOL. The analysis in this section omits the rules for the creation of new term constants and types.} For example, the reflexive law of equality in HOL states that for any term $t$ of any type $A$, we have a theorem $\vdash t = t$. By the interpretation of equality described above, under any valuation $v$, this equation is interpreted as the value $\delta_{t^{v}}(t^{v})\in\op{\tt bool}^M$, which is $\downvdash $. Hence the reflexive law preserves validity. The other rules (transitivity of equality, and so forth) are checked similarly. We may well-order each set in the collection ${\mathcal T}$. HOL posits a choice operator of type $(A\to\op{\tt bool})\to A$ for every type $A$. The well-ordering allows us to interpret HOL's choice operator as an operator that maps a function $f\in (A\to\op{\tt bool})^v$ with nonempty support to the minimal element of its support. We run through the mathematical axioms of HOL and check their validity. There are only three. The {\it axiom of infinity} positing the existence of an infinite type $I$ is logically valid by our requirement to interpret $I$ as a countably infinite set. The {\it axiom of choice} is logically valid by the well-ordering we have placed on the sets $A^M$. The {\it axiom of extensionality} also holds in this model, because it holds for sets. Thus, every axiom is logically valid. Since all axioms are logically valid and every rule of inference preserves validity, every theorem is logically valid. There is a boolean constant $\op{\tt FALSE}$ in HOL. It is defined to be the term $\forall p.~p$. An easy calculation based on its definition gives that $\op{\tt FALSE}^v = \upvdash$ for every valuation $v$. Hence, $\vdash \op{\tt FALSE}$ is not a logically valid sequent, and not a theorem. This proves HOL consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Soundness of a set-theoretic model: every rule preserves validity, every axiom is valid, and FALSE is false in the model.

nodes.name: work in ZFC
nodes.statement: We give the proof in ZFC. Here, HOL is treated purely syntactically as a set of strings in a formal language.
nodes.statement_short: Work in ZFC, treating HOL syntactically.

nodes.name: rules preserve validity
nodes.statement: We run through the rules of logic of HOL one by one and check that each one preserves validity.\footnote{There are ten such rules, giving the behavior of equality, $\lambda$-abstractions, $\beta$-reduction, and the discharge of assumptions. For reference purposes, an appendix lists the inference rules of HOL. The analysis in this section omits the rules for the creation of new term constants and types.} For example, the reflexive law of equality in HOL states that for any term $t$ of any type $A$, we have a theorem $\vdash t = t$. By the interpretation of equality described above, under any valuation $v$, this equation is interpreted as the value $\delta_{t^{v}}(t^{v})\in\op{\tt bool}^M$, which is $\downvdash $. Hence the reflexive law preserves validity. The other rules (transitivity of equality, and so forth) are checked similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Check that each inference rule (e.g. reflexivity of equality) preserves logical validity.

nodes.name: well-order and interpret choice
nodes.statement: We may well-order each set in the collection ${\mathcal T}$. HOL posits a choice operator of type $(A\to\op{\tt bool})\to A$ for every type $A$. The well-ordering allows us to interpret HOL's choice operator as an operator that maps a function $f\in (A\to\op{\tt bool})^v$ with nonempty support to the minimal element of its support.
nodes.statement_short: Well-order the sets in T to interpret the choice operator as taking minimal elements.

nodes.name: axioms are valid
nodes.statement: We run through the mathematical axioms of HOL and check their validity. There are only three. The {\it axiom of infinity} positing the existence of an infinite type $I$ is logically valid by our requirement to interpret $I$ as a countably infinite set. The {\it axiom of choice} is logically valid by the well-ordering we have placed on the sets $A^M$. The {\it axiom of extensionality} also holds in this model, because it holds for sets. Thus, every axiom is logically valid. Since all axioms are logically valid and every rule of inference preserves validity, every theorem is logically valid.
nodes.statement_short: Check the three axioms (infinity, choice, extensionality) are valid, so every theorem is valid.

nodes.name: FALSE is not a theorem
nodes.statement: There is a boolean constant $\op{\tt FALSE}$ in HOL. It is defined to be the term $\forall p.~p$. An easy calculation based on its definition gives that $\op{\tt FALSE}^v = \upvdash$ for every valuation $v$. Hence, $\vdash \op{\tt FALSE}$ is not a logically valid sequent, and not a theorem. This proves HOL consistent.
nodes.statement_short: FALSE evaluates to false, so it is not a theorem: HOL is consistent.

nodes.name: HOL Light kernel verified in HOL Light
nodes.statement: The correctness of the kernel has been formally verified, using the HOL Light proof assistant itself (extended by a large cardinal) \cite{HaSelf}.\footnote{A large cardinal axiom gives the existence of a large type corresponding to the set $\bigcup{\mathcal T}$ that we used above in the construction of a model. By G\"odel, we do not expect to construct a model of HOL in HOL except by adding an axiom to strengthen the system.} Specifically, a model of HOL can be built inside HOL itself along the same lines as the model of HOL in ZFC described above.
nodes.section: 1.4 Verification of the code that implements HOL Light
nodes.statement_short: The HOL Light kernel is formally verified in HOL Light plus a large cardinal, by building a model of HOL inside HOL.

nodes.name: Odd Order Theorem (Feit-Thompson)
nodes.statement: All finite groups of odd order are solvable.
nodes.section: 2 Advanced developments in Coq: The Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: Outline of the proof of the Odd Order theorem
nodes.statement: In very brief terms, the proof starts by assuming a minimal counterexample to the statement. This counterexample will be a finite simple group $G$ of odd order in which every proper subgroup is solvable. Each maximal subgroup of $G$ is {\it $p$-local}; that is, the normalizer of a nontrivial subgroup of $G$ of $p$-power order, for some prime $p$. The first major part of the proof of the Odd Order theorem consists in establishing restrictions on the structure of the maximal subgroups and their embeddings into $G$. In the special case when $G$ is a {\it $CN$-group} (a group whose centralizers of non-identity elements are all nilpotent), the maximal subgroups are {\it Frobenius groups} \cite{FHT}. A Frobenius group is a nontrivial semidirect product $K\rtimes H$, where $H$ is disjoint from its conjugates, and $H$ is its own normalizer \cite[Th. 7.7]{gorenstein2007finite}. In the general case, the strategy is to prove that as many of the maximal subgroups as possible are as close as possible to being Frobenius groups. This strategy encounters many exceptions and detours, but eventually the local analysis shows that the maximal subgroups are mostly Frobenius-like \cite[Sec. 16]{bender1994local}. The second major portion of the proof uses the complex character theory of $G$ to obtain inequalities over the real numbers that restrict and ultimately eliminate all possibilities for $G$. The final part of the proof uses generators and relations to remove a special case in which there are maximal subgroups isomorphic to the group of all permutations of a finite field $\ring{F}$ of the form $x \mapsto a\, \sigma (x) + b$, where $\sigma$ is a field automorphism, $a,b\in\ring{F}$, and $a$ is an element of norm $1$. It is in this part of the proof that Galois theory is most relevant.
nodes.section: 2 Advanced developments in Coq: The Odd Order theorem
nodes.statement_short: Minimal counterexample: local analysis makes maximal subgroups Frobenius-like, character theory eliminates cases, generators and relations remove the last case.

nodes.name: socle of a module
nodes.statement: For example, the socle of a module is defined as the sum of its simple submodules.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: classically
nodes.statement: The wedding of constructive and classical logics is arranged through a predicate $\op{\it classically}~\phi$ that marks every result proved by classical logic. The definition of $\op{\it classically}~\phi$ is \[ \op{classically}~\phi : Prop := \forall {b:\op{\tt bool}}, (\phi\to b) \to b. \]
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem
nodes.statement_short: The predicate classically phi is defined as: for every boolean b, (phi implies b) implies b.

nodes.name: classically as double negation
nodes.statement: When $\phi$ is quantifier free, this is essentially the usual double negation translation of a classical formula into constructive logic. The definition of {\it classically} works in such a way that $\phi$ may be used as an assumption in the proof of any boolean goal $b$, whenever $\op{\it classically}~\phi$ is known.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: function extensionality
nodes.statement: Function extensionality does not hold in Coq; that is, it is not provable that two functions are equal, if they are provably equal on every input.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: decidable equality
nodes.statement: The group theory is developed in the context of {\it finite types} with {\it decidable equality}; (that is, the type is equipped with boolean procedure that decides whether any two elements of that type are equal).
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem

nodes.name: function extensionality for finite types with decidable equality
nodes.statement: In this context, function extensionality holds and genuine quotients groups can be formed.
nodes.section: 2.2 Constructive proof of the Odd Order theorem
conclusions: function extensionality holds and genuine quotients groups can be formed

nodes.name: first-order formula with equality
nodes.statement: A {\it first-order formula with equality in the predicate calculus} is a formula built from variables $x,y,\ldots$, logical operations $\neg, \land, \Rightarrow,\ldots$, $n$-ary function symbols $f,g\ldots$, $n$-ary predicate symbols $P, Q,\ldots$ and quantified variables $\forall x, \exists y,\ldots$, according to syntactic rules that we will not spell out here.
nodes.definiendum: first-order formula with equality in the predicate calculus
nodes.statement_short: A first-order formula is built from variables, connectives, function and predicate symbols, and quantified variables.

nodes.name: example first-order formula
nodes.statement: For example, \[ ((\exists x.~P(x)) \Rightarrow (\forall y.~Q(y))) \Leftrightarrow (\forall x\forall y.~P(x)\Rightarrow Q(y)) \] is a first-order formula.

nodes.name: no quantification over function or predicate symbols
nodes.statement: In contrast to higher-order logics discussed earlier, in a first-order formula, quantifiers over function symbols and predicate symbols are not allowed.

nodes.name: refutation complete
nodes.statement: We are interested in algorithms that are {\it refutation complete}; that is, given the input of an unsatisfiable first-order formula, the algorithm outputs a proof of its unsatisfiability.

nodes.name: refutation completeness yields proofs of valid formulas
nodes.statement: A refutation complete algorithm can also produce proofs of logically valid formulas, by refuting the negation of the formula.

nodes.name: refutation completeness of resolution
nodes.statement: What has been understood for a long time are rules of inference ({\it resolution} together with special inferences that deal with equality) that are refutation complete.
conclusions: rules of inference ({\it resolution} together with special inferences that deal with equality) that are refutation complete

nodes.name: translation of higher-order problems to first-order logic
nodes.statement: There are some automated theorem provers based on higher-order logic but the most prevalent practice is to translate problems from higher-order logic into first-order logic, solve them there, then translate the answers back into higher-order logic, with an automated reconstruction of a formal proof inside the proof assistant.\footnote{There are many issues that come up in translating formulas in higher-order logic into first-order logic that I will not discuss here. In particular, some of the procedures might not be logically sound.}
nodes.statement_short: Translate higher-order goals to first-order logic, solve with a first-order prover, translate back and reconstruct a formal proof.
output: a formal proof inside the proof assistant

nodes.name: translate to FOL
nodes.statement: translate problems from higher-order logic into first-order logic,

nodes.name: solve
nodes.statement: solve them there,

nodes.name: translate back with reconstruction
nodes.statement: then translate the answers back into higher-order logic, with an automated reconstruction of a formal proof inside the proof assistant.

nodes.name: MESON procedure
nodes.statement: An early example of translating proofs in this way is Harrison's MESON procedure (based on model elimination), implemented in HOL Light. In this approach, the human supplies all the relevant theorems, and the automated procedure generates the logical glue that combines the given theorems into a proof.
nodes.statement_short: Model-elimination procedure in HOL Light: the human supplies relevant theorems and it generates the logical glue.

nodes.name: human supplies theorems
nodes.statement: the human supplies all the relevant theorems,

nodes.name: generate logical glue
nodes.statement: the automated procedure generates the logical glue that combines the given theorems into a proof.

nodes.name: sledgehammer
nodes.statement: Paulson advocates shipping the goal together with large libraries of theorems to a first-order theorem prover, and letting it figure out which of many theorems to use in the proof~\cite{Paar}. The human is no longer forced to search through the libraries to find the relevant theorems. The method is called a {\it sledgehammer} for its ability to deliver a powerful blow and its complete lack of finesse.
nodes.statement_short: Ship the goal with large theorem libraries to a first-order prover and let it choose which theorems to use.

nodes.name: ship goal and libraries
nodes.statement: shipping the goal together with large libraries of theorems to a first-order theorem prover,

nodes.name: prover selects theorems
nodes.statement: letting it figure out which of many theorems to use in the proof

nodes.name: premise selection
nodes.statement: In a refinement of this approach, an automated heuristic procedure selects a few hundred theorems deemed to be the most relevant and ships those to the theorem prover. For example, to prove a new trig identity, we might select other trig identities as likely to be relevant. There is an art to selecting relevant premises wisely, and machine learning algorithms can be trained to do this effectively \cite{urban2010evaluation}, \cite{kaliszyk2012learning}, \cite{kaliszyk2013automated}, \cite{alama2014premise}.
nodes.statement_short: Heuristically (or by machine learning) select a few hundred most relevant theorems and ship them to the prover.

nodes.name: select relevant theorems
nodes.statement: an automated heuristic procedure selects a few hundred theorems deemed to be the most relevant

nodes.name: ship to prover
nodes.statement: ships those to the theorem prover.

nodes.name: convex hull of three points has measure zero
nodes.statement: Here is one simple example of a theorem proved in this way~\cite{kaliszyk2014learning}. The theorem states that the convex hull of any three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero. The automated procedure was able to comb through large libraries of previously established theorems to locate the following relevant facts: the convex hull is a subset of the affine hull; the affine hull of three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero; and a subset of a set of measure zero has measure zero. The procedure then combines these facts with the necessary logic to give a fully automated formal proof.
nodes.statement_short: Premise selection finds three library facts that combine to prove that the convex hull of three points in R^3 has measure zero.

nodes.name: convex hull of three points in $\mathbb R^3$ has measure zero
nodes.statement: The theorem states that the convex hull of any three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero.
conclusions: the convex hull of any three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero

nodes.name: automated proof of the convex hull theorem
nodes.statement: The automated procedure was able to comb through large libraries of previously established theorems to locate the following relevant facts: the convex hull is a subset of the affine hull; the affine hull of three points in $\ring{R}^3$ is a set of measure zero; and a subset of a set of measure zero has measure zero. The procedure then combines these facts with the necessary logic to give a fully automated formal proof.
nodes.statement_short: Combine three library facts: hull subset of affine hull, affine hull has measure zero, subsets of null sets are null.

nodes.name: SAT solver
nodes.statement: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solvers implement algorithms that test for the satisfiability of formulas in propositional logic~\cite{marques2009conflict}.

nodes.name: Boolean satisfiability (SAT)
nodes.statement: Is there an assignment of truth values to propositional variables for which a given formula evaluates to true?

nodes.name: satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)
nodes.statement: SMT ({\it satisfiability modulo theories}) algorithms combine the propositional reasoning of SAT solvers with reasoning within a given theory~\cite{barrett2009satisfiability}.

nodes.name: SMT problem
nodes.statement: The input to the algorithm is a propositional formula in which the boolean variables have been replaced with predicates from the given first-order theory. An SMT algorithm searches for a valuation of the predicates in the theory that satisfies the propositional formula.
nodes.statement_short: Given a propositional formula over predicates of a first-order theory, find a valuation of the predicates satisfying it.

nodes.name: SMT case analysis in the Odd Order proof
nodes.statement: For example, the following calculation comes up in the proof of the Odd Order theorem. Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $(\beta_{ij})$ be a matrix of virtual characters, with each entry a linear combination $\pm \chi \pm \chi' \pm \chi''$ of three distinct irreducible characters. Assume the matrix has at least four rows and two columns. Assume the inner product relations \[ \langle \beta_{ij},\beta_{i'j'}\rangle = \delta_{ii'} + \delta_{jj'},\quad \text{for } (i,j)\ne (i',j'), \] with respect to the usual inner product on class functions with an orthonormal basis consisting of irreducible characters. The conclusion is that the virtual characters in each column of the matrix have a common irreducible character as constituent with a common sign. A moment's reflection reveals that it is enough to show the conclusion for arbitrary $4\times 2$ submatrices. On each $4\times 2$ block, up to renaming the irreducible characters, a finite enumeration gives all ways to express the entries $\beta_{ij}$ as a signed combination of three irreducibles. Thus, the proof reduces to a case analysis. Symmetry arguments further reduce the number of cases. The case analysis is done by hand in~\cite{peterfalvi2000character}. In the formal proof, Th\'ery programmed the claim into a quantifier-free problem with uninterpreted symbols in an SMT solver. The SMT solution was then transcribed into a formal proof in Coq~\cite{gonthier2013machine}.
nodes.statement_short: A virtual-character matrix lemma from the Odd Order proof, reduced to a finite case analysis solved by an SMT solver.

nodes.name: common constituent of virtual-character columns
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $(\beta_{ij})$ be a matrix of virtual characters, with each entry a linear combination $\pm \chi \pm \chi' \pm \chi''$ of three distinct irreducible characters. Assume the matrix has at least four rows and two columns. Assume the inner product relations \[ \langle \beta_{ij},\beta_{i'j'}\rangle = \delta_{ii'} + \delta_{jj'},\quad \text{for } (i,j)\ne (i',j'), \] with respect to the usual inner product on class functions with an orthonormal basis consisting of irreducible characters. The conclusion is that the virtual characters in each column of the matrix have a common irreducible character as constituent with a common sign.

conclusions: the virtual characters in each column of the matrix have a common irreducible character as constituent with a common sign
nodes.statement_short: In a $\ge 4\times 2$ matrix of virtual characters, each a signed sum of three irreducibles with given inner products, each column shares a signed constituent.

On each $4\times 2$ block, up to renaming the irreducible characters, a finite enumeration gives all ways to express the entries $\beta_{ij}$ as a signed combination of three irreducibles. Thus, the proof reduces to a case analysis. Symmetry arguments further reduce the number of cases. The case analysis is done by hand in~\cite{peterfalvi2000character}. In the formal proof, Th\'ery programmed the claim into a quantifier-free problem with uninterpreted symbols in an SMT solver. The SMT solution was then transcribed into a formal proof in Coq~\cite{gonthier2013machine}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to 4x2 submatrices, enumerate signed combinations up to symmetry; the case analysis is done by an SMT solver and transcribed to Coq.

nodes.name: reduce to 4x2 blocks
nodes.statement: A moment's reflection reveals that it is enough to show the conclusion for arbitrary $4\times 2$ submatrices.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to arbitrary 4x2 submatrices.

nodes.name: enumerate cases
nodes.statement: On each $4\times 2$ block, up to renaming the irreducible characters, a finite enumeration gives all ways to express the entries $\beta_{ij}$ as a signed combination of three irreducibles. Thus, the proof reduces to a case analysis.
nodes.statement_short: Finitely enumerate the signed combinations, giving a case analysis.

nodes.name: symmetry reduction
nodes.statement: Symmetry arguments further reduce the number of cases.
nodes.statement_short: Use symmetry to cut down the cases.

nodes.name: SMT solution
nodes.statement: The case analysis is done by hand in~\cite{peterfalvi2000character}. In the formal proof, Th\'ery programmed the claim into a quantifier-free problem with uninterpreted symbols in an SMT solver. The SMT solution was then transcribed into a formal proof in Coq~\cite{gonthier2013machine}.
nodes.statement_short: Cases done by hand on paper, by an SMT solver in the formal proof, transcribed into Coq.

nodes.name: reduction of integral-domain identities to Groebner bases
nodes.statement: If $S$ is any system of equalities and inequalities of polynomials that holds in every integral domain of characteristic zero, then it can be transformed into a Gr\"obner basis problem over $\ring{Q}$.
assumptions: $S$ is any system of equalities and inequalities of polynomials that holds in every integral domain of characteristic zero
conclusions: it can be transformed into a Gr\"obner basis problem over $\ring{Q}$

nodes.name: isogeny of elliptic curves by Groebner bases
nodes.statement: For example, one line of code suffices to generate a formal proof of the following isogeny of elliptic curves over $\ring{R}$. The symbol \verb!&! denotes the function embedding $\ring{N}$ into $\ring{R}$.

nodes.name: Homotopy type theory (HoTT)
nodes.statement: Homotopy type theory (HoTT) is a foundational system for mathematics that includes dependent type theory, the univalence axiom, and higher inductive types.
differentia: includes dependent type theory, the univalence axiom, and higher inductive types

nodes.name: HoTT has set quotients and function extensionality
nodes.statement: HoTT has set quotients and function extensionality, giving remedies to some of Coq's nuisances.

nodes.name: Kepler conjecture
nodes.statement: The Kepler conjecture asserts that no packing of congruent balls in $\ring{R}^3$ can have density greater than the face-centered cubic packing.
conclusions: no packing of congruent balls in $\ring{R}^3$ can have density greater than the face-centered cubic packing

nodes.name: alpha-equivalence
nodes.statement: In the following rules, we assume that $p$ and $p'$ are equal, up to a renaming of bound variables, and similarly for $b$ and $b'$. (Such terms are called $\alpha$-equivalent.)
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: reflexivity of equality (REFL)
nodes.statement: Equality is reflexive: $$ \frac{a}{\vdash a=a} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: transitivity of equality (TRANS)
nodes.statement: Equality is transitive: $$ \frac{\Gamma \vdash a=b;~~~\Delta\vdash b'=c} {\Gamma\cup\Delta \vdash a=c} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: congruence (MK_COMB)
nodes.statement: Equal functions applied to equals are equal: $$ \frac{\Gamma\vdash f=g;~~~\Delta\vdash a=b} {\Gamma\cup\Delta\vdash f\hskip0.1em a = g\hskip0.1em b} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: abstraction (ABS)
nodes.statement: The rule of abstraction holds. Equal function bodies give equal functions: $$ \frac{x;~~~\Gamma\vdash a=b} {\Gamma \vdash \lambda x.\ a~=\lambda x.\ b} ~\hbox{\ (if $x$ is not free in $\Gamma$)} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: beta-reduction (BETA)
nodes.statement: The application of the function $x\mapsto a$ to $x$ gives $a$: $$ \frac{(\lambda x.~a)\, x} {\vdash (\lambda x.\ a)\, x = a} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: assumption rule (ASSUME)
nodes.statement: Assume $p$, then conclude $p$: $$ \frac{p\hbox{:} bool} {p \vdash p} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: equality-based modus ponens (EQ_MP)
nodes.statement: An `equality-based' rule of modus ponens holds: $$ \frac{\Gamma\vdash p;~~~\Delta \vdash p'=q} {\Gamma\cup \Delta \vdash q} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: deduction antisymmetry (DEDUCT_ANTISYM)
nodes.statement: If the assumption $q$ gives conclusion $p$ and the assumption $p$ gives $q$, then they are equivalent: $$ \frac{\Gamma \vdash p;~~~\Delta\vdash q} {(\Gamma\setminus q)\cup (\Delta\setminus p) \vdash p=q} $$
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: type variable substitution (INST_TYPE)
nodes.statement: Type variable substitution holds. If arbitrary types are substituted in parallel for type variables in a sequent, a theorem results.
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL

nodes.name: term variable substitution (INST)
nodes.statement: Term variable substitution holds. If arbitrary terms are substituted in parallel for term variables in a sequent, a theorem results.
nodes.section: 6 Appendix. The inference rules of HOL
